problem: Source: the cheerful room only 'in some measure effaced the eerie impression' (partial). MODERN 'gradually erased' implies the impression was fully erased, dropping the hedge.
new_text: After Mrs. Fairfax bid me a kind good night, I locked my door and looked around the room at a leisurely pace. The cheerful appearance of my little room partly erased the eerie impression left by that wide hall, that dark and cavernous staircase, and that long, cold gallery. I remembered that after a day of physical exhaustion and mental worry, I was at last in a safe harbor. Gratitude swelled my heart. I knelt by the bedside and gave thanks where thanks were due, not forgetting to ask for guidance on the road ahead, and for the strength to deserve the kindness so freely offered before I had earned it. My bed held no thorns that night, and my solitary room held no fears. Weary and content at once, I slept quickly and deeply. When I woke, it was broad daylight.

problem: The repair restoring source 'would not at least recoil from me with antipathy' produced the ungrammatical 'my new pupil wouldn't at least recoil from me in dislike'; word order should be 'would at least not recoil'.
new_text: I got up and dressed with care. I was obliged to dress plainly—every article of clothing I owned was made with extreme simplicity—but I was by nature careful about my appearance. It wasn't my habit to be careless about how I looked or the impression I made. On the contrary, I always wanted to look as well as I could, and to please as much as my lack of beauty would allow. I sometimes regretted that I wasn't prettier. I sometimes wished for rosy cheeks, a straight nose, and a small, shapely mouth. I wished I were tall, stately, and well-proportioned. I felt it was a misfortune to be so small, so pale, and to have such irregular, striking features. And why did I have these wishes and regrets? It would be hard to say—I couldn't clearly explain it to myself at the time, though I had a reason, a logical, natural one. In any case, once I had brushed my hair very smooth and put on my black dress—which, Quaker-like as it was, at least had the virtue of fitting perfectly—and straightened my clean white collar, I thought I would look respectable enough for Mrs. Fairfax, and that my new pupil would at least not recoil from me in dislike. Having opened my window and checked that everything on the dressing table was neat and tidy, I ventured out.

problem: Source: 'it _was_ an incident of no moment, no romance, no interest in a sense'. MODERN 'nothing special, really—no drama, no romance, no particular interest' loses the emphatic concession ('it was'), the hedge 'in a sense' (which sets up 'yet it marked with change...'), and replaces 'no moment' (no importance) with 'no drama'.
new_text: I picked up my muff and walked on. The incident had happened and was gone. It was an incident of no importance, no romance, no interest in a sense. Yet it marked a change in one single hour of a monotonous life. My help had been needed and asked for. I had given it. I was pleased to have done something—trivial and fleeting as it was, it had been an act, and I was tired of a purely passive existence. The new face, too, was like a new picture added to the gallery of my memory, and it was unlike any of the others hanging there. First, because it was male. And second, because it was dark, strong, and stern. I still had it before me when I reached Hay and slipped the letter into the post office. I saw it as I walked fast downhill all the way home. When I reached the stile, I paused, looked around, and listened, half-expecting to hear a horse's hooves ring on the path again, and to see a cloaked rider and a Gytrash-like Newfoundland dog appear once more. I saw only the hedge and a pollard willow before me, standing still and straight against the moonlight. I heard only the faintest breath of wind stirring fitfully among the trees around Thornfield, a mile away. And when I glanced toward the sound, my eye caught a light kindling in a window of the hall. It reminded me I was late, and I hurried on.
